Grieving today with change in policy that'll severely impact my business

Lost a chunk of my business today with the change in a policy in my industry

It's a complicated story - 

2 years ago there was also a change in policy, and I thought it was the end, and I was also severely burned out. So I decided to stop and just take a break.

Then about 4 months ago, I came across a business idea which felt excellent to do, and I tried to launch it to no avail. But after many attempts, it's finally likely to launch within the next 2-3 weeks.

In these 4 months, I also went through several rounds of medical treatment, finally finished, and then came down with a horrible fever and infection for another few weeks. It wasn't like I was sick per se, it's just that I decided to finally get certain procedures done-- and they somehow wiped me out completely.

Just grieving a little as it really showed me what opportunity cost looks like. The idea that I sat with for months, that didn't get implemented, really cost me quite a lot.

I came back from a round of burnout and depression and being lost, after 2 years, to find myself turning 40 - and still having to work. Something I could have gotten out of, if I had made better decisions. I could be focusing on building my family, taking holidays, having kids now... but instead I'm rebuilding these businesses and feeling grief and regretful.

In the past 2 months, it felt like I suddenly gained clarity on career. I term it as "fog being lifted" and indeed had been working endlessly. Even with a 3 week long fever. I could have launched this just a bit sooner, before the policy killed everything. But nope, it's still not launched yet.

On top of that, today is a special kind of anniversary, that reminded me of what (who) I lost - and in a way, how I should never have met the wrong person. I know this became a personal rant, but dealing with personal grief affects work and business so much.

Exactly 2 years ago, I also asked myself the same question on Reddit - "What's the point of money and life, if there's no one to share with" - and sad to say, I've returned to the same exact question. I guess the main difference now is that I'm determined to turn things out.

I've actually tried to work and change things for the last 9 months now (all of this year) and I feel like things just got so much harder. 2 of my personal goals got badly affected by policy changes - one affects me getting a house (personal), the other one is the business that just couldn't, wouldn't work.

For now, I can only:

1. Get over this, move on, do what I can now, look forward, work harder and smarter, make better decisions, and/or

2. Lower my expectations in life

  
Rebuilding businesses is hard enough. To do it while grieving and lonely, and getting over one physical challenge after another, is a whole level of challenge.

where do you draw the line between quoting a job and designing it for free?

I’m involved in my family's marble business.

Most of our traditional work is straightforward enough to quote, slabs, dimensions, finish, quantity, transport, etc.

But we've started taking on more custom marble fabrication and finished-product enquiries, and I'm running into a problem I hadn't appreciated before.

Someone sends us a photograph of an object and says:

**“Can you make this in marble? What would it cost?”**

To the customer, that's a request for a price.

For us, answering it properly might mean figuring out:

Will the design even work in stone?

What thickness will stop it breaking?

Can the inside actually be machined?

Does it need two pieces rather than one?

How will hardware be fixed?

Will it stand safely?

How much hand finishing will it need?

How do we pack it?

And only after all of that can we estimate cost properly.

By that point, we've sometimes done a meaningful amount of product development for someone who may have casually sent the same image to ten manufacturers.

But I don't want to swing too far the other way either.

If somebody sends a simple enquiry and gets back a form asking 18 questions plus a design fee, we've created friction before they even know whether the project is remotely in budget.

For people doing custom fabrication/manufacturing — furniture, metalwork, millwork, stone, signage, etc. — how do you handle this?

I'm considering something like:

very rough feasibility + price range for free,

then paid prototyping/engineering once the customer wants an accurate quote, with the fee credited against a production order.

Does that work in practice?

Where do you personally draw the line between **sales effort** and **unpaid engineering**?

>• Automate 70%+ of customer acquisition/marketing activities

Business Owners: STAY AWAY from Hibu Marketing. Consider this your warning.

**Business Owners: STAY AWAY from Hibu Marketing. Consider this your warning.**  
I cannot believe how absolutely awful my experience with Hibu has been. If you’re a small business owner considering them, PLEASE do your homework before signing anything.  
The salesperson told me everything I wanted to hear to get my signature. I specifically requested $3,000/month toward Google Ads. I was told 100% would go toward advertising because Hibu “makes their money elsewhere.” Turns out only about $1,500 was actually allocated to Google Ads, with the rest going toward other services.  
I was also told I could change my Google Ads budget at any time. That turned out to be another promise that wasn’t honored.  
And their supposedly “custom” websites? I discovered another auto repair shop IN MY SAME CITY, with the SAME SALESPERSON, had essentially the same website, right down to the stock photo!  
I’ve had TWO website services canceled and an SEO package terminated after numerous issues.  
The incompetence and lack of communication have been unbelievable. In my experience, if you actually care about your business, plan on babysitting everything, catching mistakes yourself, and doing the work you’re supposedly paying these people to handle.  
Here’s the part that absolutely blows my mind.  
**I FIRED THEM. I hired another company. I told Hibu to stop advertising my business. I even sent a cease-and-desist.**  
Their response? They refuse to terminate my Google Ads contract. Instead, they’ve repeatedly offered me credits toward services I have made abundantly clear I DO NOT WANT.  
**It’s MY business. MY reputation. And I no longer want this company representing either one.**  
I’ve never encountered a company so determined to hold on to an unhappy customer rather than simply part ways.  
I’m sharing my experience because I wish someone had warned me before I signed. Get EVERY sales promise in writing, demand a breakdown of where every advertising dollar goes, and read the cancellation terms carefully.  
**My experience with Hibu has been an absolute nightmare. Other small business owners deserve to know what they’re potentially signing up for.**
